Summary of the Repealing and Amending (Second) Act, 2015
Objectives of the Act
•	To repeal obsolete, redundant, and spent Central Acts that no longer serve any practical purpose. 
•	To make minor consequential amendments to existing laws, including corrections of statutory references, drafting errors, and inconsistencies. 
•	To simplify and modernise the corpus of Central legislation. 
•	To improve the clarity, accessibility, and efficiency of the legal framework. 
Key Provisions
•	Repeal of Enactments: The Act repeals a number of Central Acts and amending Acts that had become obsolete, fully implemented, superseded, or otherwise unnecessary. 
•	Consequential Amendments: It makes limited amendments to certain existing enactments to update references, rectify drafting errors, and ensure consistency in statutory language. 
•	Saving Clause: The repeal of any enactment does not affect its previous operation or any rights, obligations, liabilities, penalties, investigations, or legal proceedings arising under it, unless expressly provided otherwise. 
•	Schedules: The Acts repealed and the amendments made are specified in the Schedules to the Act.

Summary of the Advocates Act, 1961
Key Provisions
1.	Bar Council of India (BCI)
•	Establishes the Bar Council of India, the apex statutory body for the legal profession.
•	Its functions include:
•	Prescribing standards of professional conduct and etiquette.
•	Promoting and supervising legal education.
•	Recognizing law degrees for enrolment.
•	Protecting the rights and interests of advocates.
•	Exercising disciplinary and supervisory powers over State Bar Councils.
2.	State Bar Councils
•	Constitutes State Bar Councils for each State or group of States.
•	Their functions include:
•	Enrolling advocates.
•	Maintaining the State roll of advocates.
•	Safeguarding the rights and welfare of advocates.
•	Conducting disciplinary proceedings against advocates.
3.	Enrolment of Advocates
•	Prescribes the qualifications and conditions for enrolment as an advocate.
•	A person enrolled with a State Bar Council becomes entitled to practice law, subject to the provisions of the Act and the rules made under it.
4.	Right to Practice
•	Advocates enrolled under the Act have the right to practice before:
•	All courts in India.
•	Tribunals.
•	Any authority legally authorized to take evidence.
•	The exercise of this right is subject to the Act and applicable rules.
5.	Professional Conduct and Discipline
•	Advocates are required to maintain high standards of professional ethics.
•	Complaints of professional or other misconduct are inquired into by the disciplinary committees of the State Bar Councils.
•	Appeals against disciplinary orders may lie to the Bar Council of India and, in appropriate cases, to the Supreme Court.
6.	Legal Education
•	The Bar Council of India is empowered to:
•	Lay down standards of legal education.
•	Recognize universities and law degrees for enrolment.
•	Conduct inspections of law institutions.
7.	Senior Advocates
•	Provides for the designation of distinguished advocates as Senior Advocates by the Supreme Court or High Courts.
•	Senior Advocates are subject to certain restrictions regarding legal practice as prescribed by the rules.
8.	Rule-making Powers
•	The Bar Council of India and State Bar Councils may frame rules on:
•	Professional conduct and etiquette.
•	Legal education.
•	Enrolment procedures.
•	Disciplinary proceedings.
•	Welfare measures for advocates.

indexableObject.name: Agreement void where both parties are under mistake as to matter of fact.

dc.identifier.section_page_note.value:
Where both the parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is void.
Explanation.--An erroneous opinion as to the value of the thing which forms the subject-matter of the agreement, is not to be deemed a mistake as to a matter of fact.
Illustrations
(a) A agrees to sell to B a specific cargo of goods supposed to be on its way from England to Bombay. It turns out that, before the day of the bargain, the ship conveying the cargo had been cast away and the goods lost. Neither party was aware of the these facts. The agreement is void.
(b) A agrees to buy from B a certain horse. It turns out that the horse was dead at the time of the bargain, though neither party was aware of the fact. The agreement is void.
(c) A, being entitled to an estate for the life of B, agrees to sell it to C. B was dead at the time of the agreement, but both parties were ignorant of the fact. The agreement is void.
